imperial.name: Kale

actions.text:
Sow

Mar–Jun. After early crops, Jun–early Jul.

Transplant

Apr–Jul. Late sowings often Jul–early Aug if there is time to establish.

methods.text:
Sow 

Scatter seed thinly in a nursery bed or start in modules. Cover lightly and thin crowded seedlings. Rape kale can be sown in place and thinned in stages.

Transplant 

Water the nursery row before lifting. Move sturdy plants at 4–6 in. tall. Harden off plants raised under cover. Set lowest leaves just above the soil, firm and water. Allow 18–24 in. between rows for full-sized plants.

varieties.text:
MODERN AND COLOURED
Nero di Toscana

A dark, strap-leaved kale for repeated picking. Its textured leaves are especially useful in soups, stews and winter cooking.

CURLY-LEAVED
Reflex F1

A green curly kale for productive winter picking. A useful maincrop choice where familiar curled leaves are preferred.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Red Russian

A flat-leaved kale with purple stems and tender young leaves. Useful for salads when young and cooking when larger.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Redbor F1

A purple-red curly kale that adds colour to the plot. Pick regularly for tender leaves and continued growth.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Yurok F1

A dark-leaved kale in the Tuscan style. Retain as a modern alternative where this leaf shape is preferred.

Kale.
DIFFICULTY
Fairly Easy
2/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Autumn / Winter

Kale, or borecole, produces leaves and spring shoots instead of a heart. Varieties range from curled green leaves to red or flat-leaved types. It stands through autumn and winter, and the leaves often taste sweeter after frost.

Quick facts
Germination

7–12 days

Sowing depth

about 1/2 in.

Row spacing

6 in. between seed rows

Yield per plant

2 lb

Plant spacing

About 18 in. between standard plants; allow more room for large varieties. Follow the packet for compact or baby-leaf crops.

Sow

Mar–Jun. After early crops, Jun–early Jul.

Transplant

Apr–Jul. Late sowings often Jul–early Aug if there is time to establish.

Harvest

Sep – Apr

Ready in

First picking depends on variety and leaf size; main crops give autumn/winter leaves and later spring shoots.

Recommended varieties
MODERN AND COLOURED
Nero di Toscana

A dark, strap-leaved kale for repeated picking. Its textured leaves are especially useful in soups, stews and winter cooking.

CURLY-LEAVED
Reflex F1

A green curly kale for productive winter picking. A useful maincrop choice where familiar curled leaves are preferred.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Red Russian

A flat-leaved kale with purple stems and tender young leaves. Useful for salads when young and cooking when larger.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Redbor F1

A purple-red curly kale that adds colour to the plot. Pick regularly for tender leaves and continued growth.

MODERN AND COLOURED
Yurok F1

A dark-leaved kale in the Tuscan style. Retain as a modern alternative where this leaf shape is preferred.

Key risks
Cabbage caterpillars

Caterpillars of cabbage white butterfly, cabbage moth and related pests chew holes in leaves.

Club root (finger and toe)

Swollen, distorted roots cause poor growth and wilting in sunshine.

Cabbage whitefly

Small white-winged insects and scale-like young live below brassica leaves; adults fly up when disturbed.

Mealy aphid

Large clusters of waxy, greyish 'greenflies' occur on the underside of leaves and tips of plants from June onwards in hot, dry weather.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
58
BRASSICAS

Fertile, settled soil

Drain well; firm transplants.

Keep plants steady

Water; prevent wind rock.

Spring feeding

Feed only weak spring growth.

Soil & preparation
Choose sun or light shade and well-drained soil. Kale tolerates many soils but yields best in fertile ground.
Follow early crops; weed and add mature compost as needed. Use settled or no-dig soil. Firm transplants without compacting wet ground.
Sowing & planting
Raise young plants
Set deeper and firm
Sow 

Scatter seed thinly in a nursery bed or start in modules. Cover lightly and thin crowded seedlings. Rape kale can be sown in place and thinned in stages.

Transplant 

Water the nursery row before lifting. Move sturdy plants at 4–6 in. tall. Harden off plants raised under cover. Set lowest leaves just above the soil, firm and water. Allow 18–24 in. between rows for full-sized plants.

Looking after the crop
Weed carefully and water young plants. Check and secure loose stems after windy weather, without treading heavily on wet soil.
Remove yellow leaves, earth up in autumn and stake tall plants on exposed sites.
Support insect-proof mesh where needed and secure bird protection. Keep covers clear of leaves and check beneath them; leaf colour gives no immunity.
Give an organic liquid feed only if spring growth is weak.
Harvesting & storage
Pick tender outer leaves little and often. Leave the growing top and enough foliage for repeat crops; reject tough or yellow leaves.
Pick young, tender side shoots in late winter and spring, usually about 4–5 in. long; timing varies with variety and weather. Removing a mature crown encourages shoots; this is a separate method, not routine leaf picking.
Pick Red Russian leaves young; baby-leaf harvest is not limited to spring. Chop healthy finished stems into short 4–6 in. pieces to help them compost; follow disease guidance for affected roots.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Cabbage caterpillars	Holes; feeding caterpillars.	Hand-pick eggs and larvae; use fine mesh.
Club root (finger and toe)	Swollen roots; wilting.	Avoid infected soil; clean tools. Test before liming; no cure.
Cabbage whitefly	White flies under leaves.	Tolerate minor colonies; encourage natural enemies.
Mealy aphid	Grey colonies; curled leaves.	Squash damaging colonies; encourage predators.
Pigeons	Pecked or stripped leaves.	Net securely, clear of leaves.
Slugs and snails	Holes; seedlings eaten.	Hand-pick at dusk; clear yellow leaves near seedlings.
Cabbage root fly	Wilting; tunnelled roots.	Use collars or mesh on a rotated bed.
Flea beetle	Tiny holes; jumping beetles.	Mesh young plants; keep growth steady.
Final tips

Match spacing to variety and method; give larger plants more room.

Winter-worn plants may still provide tender spring shoots.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 106–111 · Growing Techniques 149–151
